hit.profile_notes:
According to United States - Environmental Protection Agency; March 04, 2026: On March 04, 2026, A complaint filed against Canada Holdings LLC (F/k/a Lafarge North America, Inc. and others alleging each of the defendants own or operate, owned or operated, or arranged for disposal or treatment, or arranged with a transporter for transport for disposal or treatment, of hazardous substances for, at least one facility and/or vessel at the Site as defined in Section 101(9) & (28) of CERCLA, 42 U.S.C. § 9601(9) & (28) and RCW 70A.305.020(24). 

The United States has undertaken response actions to address the release or threatened release of hazardous substances at or from the Site. In undertaking the response actions, the United States has incurred and will continue to incur response costs as defined in Section 101(25) of CERCLA, 42 U.S.C. § 9601(25). EPA has determined that the hazardous substances at the Site present significant risks to human health and the environment, and that response actions are necessary to abate a danger or threat.

According to United States Attorney - Western District of New York; October 31, 2012: Published on that date, Lafarge North America, Inc., (LNA), a national supplier of building and construction materials and manufacturer of concrete and concrete products, has paid USD 950,000 to the United States to resolve potential civil claims by the United States under the False Claims Act. 

The matter involved highway construction projects in the Western District of New York which were funded, in part, by federal funds via the Federal Highway Administration (FHWA). This required that a certain percentage of the work be performed by Disadvantaged Business Enterprises (DBE). Rayford Enterprises, Inc., d/b/a Rayford Concrete Products, a Buffalo company, was awarded subcontracts on these construction projects based on its representations that it was a DBE manufacturer of concrete. Rayford was not, in fact, a manufacturer of concrete, nor did the company have a concrete batching facility or other equipment necessary to manufacture concrete. Instead, Rayford had an agreement with Lafarge North America to manufacture and deliver concrete for these projects. Lafarge North America is not a DBE.

According to United States Department of Justice and United States Environmental Protection Agency; November 29, 2011: Published on that date, Lafarge North America Inc. agrees to pay USD 740,000 Penalty to Resolve Clean Water Act Violations in Five States. Lafarge North America Inc., one of the largest suppliers of construction materials in the United States and Canada, and four of its U.S. subsidiaries have agreed to resolve alleged Clean Water Act violations. The violations include unpermitted discharges of stormwater and failure to comply with stormwater permits at 21 stone, gravel, sand, asphalt and ready-mix concrete facilities in Alabama, Colorado, Georgia, Maryland and New York.  Stormwater flowing over concrete manufacturing facilities can carry debris, sediment and pollutants including pesticides, petroleum products, chemicals and solvents, which can have a significant impact on water quality.

Lafarge will implement a nationwide evaluation and compliance program at 189 of its similar facilities in the United States to ensure they meet Clean Water Act requirements. Lafarge will also pay a penalty of USD 740,000 and implement two supplemental environmental projects, in which the company will complete conservation easements to protect approximately 166 acres in Maryland and Colorado. The value of the land has been appraised at USD 2,950,000. Lafarge will also implement one state environmentally beneficial project to support environmental training for state inspectors. The state project is valued at USD 10,000.

According to United States Environmental Protection Agency; January 21, 2010: On January 21, 2015, United States filed Clean Air Act settlement with Lafarge North America, Inc. to reduce air emissions from container glass and Portland cement plants throughout the country. The settlements covers all 13 U.S. plants owned by the Lafarge Company and two subsidiaries, the nation’s second largest manufacturer of Portland cement.

Lafarge has also agreed to pay a civil penalty of USD 5,075,000 within 30 days of entry of the consent decree. USD 3,383,000 will be paid to the United States, and the remainder will be paid to the state and local agencies participating in the settlement.

According to United States - Maryland Attorney General; May 13, 2009: Published on that date, the State of Maryland has filed suit against Lafarge North America for water pollution violations at its Texas Quarry in Cockeysville. The complaint filed in the Circuit Court for Baltimore County alleges 413 violations of Maryland’s water pollution laws at the concrete production and limestone quarry. Each violation carries a maximum penalty of USD 10,000.

The Texas Quarry is a surface mine operated by Lafarge and mined primarily for construction aggregate. On or about March 21, 2007, it is alleged that Lafarge discharged several tons of aggregate, crushed stone, and stone dust into nearby Goodwin Run a tributary of Gunpowder Falls and its floodplain. The amount of material discharged ranged in depth from four to 18 inches and reduced the width of the stream from approximately 15 feet wide to less than four feet wide.
sources: US-United States Attorney - Western District of New York

hit.name: LaFarge, Corp.
hit.position_or_allegation: Agreed to pay USD 1,500,000 for engaging in environmental crimes - September 28, 2000.

details.enforcement: Environmental Crimes/Disciplined | US-U.S. Federal Trade Commission | United States

hit.profile_notes:
According to United Stated-Michigan Attorney General; September 28, 2000: On September 28, 2000, The Department of Environmental Quality, Michigan announced that the Lafarge Corporation has agreed to settle an air pollution enforcement action resulting from the operation of its Portland cement manufacturing plant in Alpena. As a result of the settlement, the company has agreed to reduce emissions of hydrogen chloride (HCl) from its Portland cement kilns and to control dust levels around the facility.

Lafarge will pay more than USD 1,500,000 to install the control measures required by the settlement and will pay the State of Michigan USD 723,000 in penalties and fines.

According to United Stated-Federal Trade Commission; October 16, 1998: On October 16, 1998, LaFarge, Corp. has agreed to restructure its agreement to purchase certain assets of Holnam, Inc., to settle Federal Trade Commission charges that the purchase agreement violated federal antitrust laws and could drive up prices for cement in the Pacific Northwest. LaFarge Corp. is based in Reston, Virginia. It is one of the largest suppliers of cement for residential, commercial, institutional and public works construction, with 14 plants in the United States and Canada and sales of USD 1600000 in 1996. Holnam, headquartered in Dundee, Michigan, is the number one supplier of cement in the United States. It operates 19 cement plants in North America and had sales of USD 983000000 in 1996.

According to United Stated-Federal Trade Commission; October 16, 1998: On October 16, 1998, The Federal Trade Commission issued Complaint against Lafarge, S.A  having reason to believe that the Lafarge, S.A controls, Lafarge Corporation (collectively "Respondents"), has entered into an agreement to acquire cement production assets of Holnam, Inc., that the agreement violates Section 5 of the Federal Trade Commission Act, as amended, 15 U.S.C.  45, and that the acquisition, if consummated, would result in a violation of Section 5 of the Federal Trade Commission Act, as amended, 15 U.S.C. 45, and Section 7 of the Clayton Act, as amended, 15 U.S.C.  18, and it appearing to the Commission that a proceeding in respect thereof would be in the public interest, hereby issues its complaint,

THE PROPOSED ACQUISITION: On February 4, 1998, Lafarge and Holnam signed a Letter of Intent setting out the principal elements of a proposed transaction, whereby Lafarge would acquire Holnam's Seattle, Washington cement plant and related assets.

relationships: Purdue Pharma of North Carolina L.P. (AffiliatedCompany
hit.profile_notes:
According to the U.S. Florida Attorney General, U.S. North Dakota Attorney General and U.S. Texas Attorney General; May 15, 2018: A lawsuit was filed against Purdue Pharma L.P. for allegedly using a campaign of misrepresentations and omissions about the use of opioids to doctors and consumers in order to increase prescriptions and opioid use, including false statements about the addictive nature of opioids and omissions of the severe risks posed by taking opioids. 

The opioid distributors allegedly shipped inordinately high volumes of opioids to customers in Florida and failed to report these suspicious orders of opioids, thereby fueling widespread diversion of opioids throughout the state. In the complaint filed the defendants’ actions violated the Florida Deceptive and Unfair Trade Practices Act, the Florida RICO Act, and violated common law public nuisance and negligence.

hit.profile_notes:
According to U.S. Federal Trade Commission; April 26, 2012: A telemarketing operation that allegedly deceived consumers who were trying to sell their timeshare properties is permanently banned from the timeshare resale and rental business, and from all telemarketing, under settlements with the Federal Trade Commission. The case is part of the FTC's ongoing effort to crack down on con artists who use fraud and deception to take advantage of consumers in financial distress. The settlement order against David S. Taylor contains the same conduct prohibitions and imposes a USD 3.7 million judgment, which was suspended based on his inability to pay.

According to U.S. Federal Trade Commission; March 31, 2011: At the Federal Trade Commission’s request, a federal district court has issued a temporary restraining order against a Florida-based telemarketing scheme that allegedly tricked timeshare owners who sought to sell their timeshare properties. According to the FTC’s complaint, since at least 2006, Vacation Property Services, Inc., two related companies, and their three principals have made tens of thousands of unsolicited telemarketing calls to timeshare owners claiming that they could quickly find buyers for the owners’ timeshares. The defendants allegedly trick consumers into paying large up-front fees, typically using one of two deceptive sales pitches – that they have buyers lined up and waiting to buy the timeshare properties or that they will find a buyer for the timeshare properties within a short period of time. Regardless of the pitch used, the defendants demand that consumers pay an up-front fee, ranging from USD 200 to more than USD 8,000. The FTC’s complaint charges the defendants with violating the FTC Act and the Telemarketing Sales Rule by misrepresenting their refund policies and the existence of potential buyers. The complaint also charges the defendants with calling hundreds of thousands of consumers between November 2009 and November 2010 whose phone numbers are on the FTC’s Do Not Call Registry. In addition to Vacation Property Services, Inc., the complaint names Vacation Property Sellers, Inc., doing business as (d/b/a) Timeshare Experts; Higher Level Marketing, Inc., d/b/a Vacation Property Services; Albert M. Wilson; David S. Taylor; and Frank M. Perry, Jr.

hit.profile_notes:
According to United States - Illinois Investment Policy Board - Prohibited Investment List; Danske Bank, is removed from the Illinois Prohibited Investment List. The company was previously included in the list, deemed prohibited from investment.

According to the Financial Supervisory Authority of Norway; January 22, 2025: On January 15, 2025: the Norwegian Financial Supervisory Authority has imposed a fine against Danske Bank A/S worth NOK 50,000,000 for market manipulation in connection with the issuance of a government bond in February 2023. The Financial Supervisory Authority of Norway believes that the bank allegedly drove up the swap rate, which impacted the bond’s price and yield, and that the trades were carried out based on a deliberate strategy and in a situation where the bank profited from a high effective yield.

Аccording to the French Judicial Public Interest Agreements List; September 18, 2024: On September 18, 2024, the Paris court confirmed the judicial public interest agreement between the Paris Prosecutor's Office and Danske Bank A/S signed on August 27, 2024. A judicial investigation was opened on April 09, 2015 into organized laundering of tax fraud and concealment of organized fraud committed since January 01, 2008. It revealed that the bank's Estonian branch transferred the proceeds of tax fraud committed by an executive of a French company. Danske Bank A/S agreed to pay EUR 6,328,799 to settle the charges. 

According to storage.courtlistener.com: On January 05, 2023, Danske Bank A/S was sentenced to three years of probation for conspiracy to commit bank fraud.

According to the United States Attorney - Southern District of New York and United States Department of Justice; December 13, 2022: On December 13, 2022, Danske Bank A/S pleaded guilty to conspiring to commit bank fraud and agreed to forfeit USD 2,000,000,000 to resolve the United States investigation into Danske Bank’s fraud on U.S. banks. According to court documents, Danske Bank defrauded U.S. banks regarding Danske Bank Estonia’s customers and anti-money laundering controls to facilitate access to the U.S. financial system for Danske Bank Estonia’s high-risk customers, who resided outside of Estonia – including in Russia. The Justice Department will credit nearly USD 850,000,000 in payments that Danske Bank makes to resolve related parallel investigations by other domestic and foreign authorities. Additionally, the SEC announced a separate settlement with Danske Bank. Under the terms of that resolution, Danske Bank agreed to pay approximately USD 413,000,000, which includes a civil monetary penalty of USD 178,600,000, as well as disgorgement that will be credited to any such payments made to the Danish authorities or the department in connection with Danske Bank’s guilty plea.

According to the United States Securities and Exchange Commission; December 13, 2022: On December 13, 2022, the Securities and Exchange Commission announced fraud charges against Danske Bank for misleading investors about its anti-money laundering (AML) compliance program in its Estonian branch and failing to disclose the risks posed by the program’s significant deficiencies. Danske Bank agreed to pay USD 413,000,000 to settle the SEC’s charges.  The Securities and Exchange Commission entered a final judgment permanently enjoining Danske Bank from future violations and ordered Danske Bank to pay USD 178,600,000 in disgorgement, USD 55,800,000 in prejudgment interest, and USD 178,600,000 in a civil penalty.  According to the SEC’s complaint, when Danske Bank acquired its Estonian branch in 2007, it knew or should have known that a substantial portion of the branch’s customers were engaging in transactions that had a high risk of involving money laundering; that its internal risk management procedures were inadequate to prevent such activity; and that its AML and Know-Your-Customer procedures were not being followed and did not comply with applicable laws and rules. The SEC alleges that, from 2009 to 2016, these high-risk customers, none of whom were residents of Estonia, utilized Danske Bank’s services to transact billions of dollars in suspicious transactions through the U.S. and other countries, generating as much as 99 percent of the Estonian branch’s profits. The complaint further alleges that, although Danske Bank knew of these high-risk transactions, it made materially misleading statements and omissions in its publicly available reports stating that it complied with its AML obligations and that it had effectively managed its AML risks.

According to the Central Bank of Ireland; September 15, 2022: On September 13, 2022, the Central Bank of Ireland (the Central Bank) reprimanded and fined Danske Bank A/S, trading in Ireland as Danske Bank, EUR 1,820,000 pursuant to its Administrative Sanctions Procedure for three breaches of the Criminal Justice (Money Laundering & Terrorist Financing) Act 2010, as amended (the CJA). The three CJA breaches stem from the failure by Danske Bank A/S (Danske) to ensure that its automated transaction monitoring system monitored the transactions of certain categories of customers of its Irish branch, for a period of almost nine years, between 2010 and 2019. The root cause of this failure was historic data filters that were applied within Danske’s automated transaction monitoring system, first implemented in 2005 and rolled out to the Irish branch in 2006. Danske failed to consider the appropriateness of these historic data filters within the system or make any adjustments to the system to take account of the specific requirements of the CJA when it came into force in Ireland in 2010. This led to the erroneous exclusion of certain categories of customers from transaction monitoring, including some customers rated by Danske as high and medium risk, which caused the three breaches of the CJA in this case. The Central Bank has determined the appropriate fine to be EUR 2,600,000, which has been reduced by 30% to EUR 1,820,000 in accordance with the early settlement discount scheme provided for in the Central Bank’s Administrative Sanctions Procedure (ASP). 

According to bnn-news.com; December 16, 2020: As of December 2020, Danske Bank A/S is under investigation by US Department of the Treasury, Federal Bureau of Investigations and the US Attorney’s Office in New York over suspicions of money laundering and fraud. Danske Bank A/S has previously reported being under investigation by USA authorities for its suspicious flow of money through their branches in Baltic States.

According to the United States - CBOE Futures Exchange - CFE; January 16, 2020: On January 16, 2020, Danske Bank A/S has been ordered to pay USD 30,000 in penalty for violation of CFE rules. From in or about November 2018 to in or about January 2019, including on six trade dates, Danske submitted simultaneous buy and sell orders in the same VX futures contract expiration at the identical price for the same account. Danske submitted the matching orders in order to rebalance different sub-strategies in the account.

According to challenges.fr and danskebank.com; February 07, 2019: On February 07, 2019, Danske Bank A/S was placed under investigation in Paris, France in connection with an investigation into organized laundering of tax evasion proceeds. Reportedly, between 2007 and 2014, Danske Bank A/S might have assisted in multiple transactions consisting in investing, concealing, or converting the direct or indirect proceeds of the offenses for non-resident customers of Danske Bank’s branch in Estonia. The investigation covers transactions amounting to EUR 21,600,000. Danske Bank A/S was placed under investigation for the first time on October 11, 2017, then the bank was assigned "an assisted witness" status on January 25, 2018. 

According to irishexaminer.com; December 04, 2018: On December 2018, Danske Bank was required by the Danish Financial Supervisory Authority to add the sum of EUR 1,300,000,000 to its capital requirement so as to be prepared to alleviate the consequences of the money laundering scandal.

According to thelocal.dk; November 28, 2018: In November, 2018 Danske Bank was charged with violating money-laundering laws between February, 2007 and January, 2016. The Copenhagen international financial crimes unit SØIK reported that the investigation begun in August offered the ground for the charges.

According to reuters.com; October 04, 2018: Published on that date, Danske Bank A/S is under criminal investigation by United States authorities over a USD 230,000,000,000 money laundering scandal at its Estonian branch. The internal report of the bank said that misconduct stretching from 2007 to 2015 at the Estonian branch payments totaling USD 230,000,000,000, many of which it described as suspicious. Denmark’s Estonian branch were held by entities or individuals in Russia, which is the subject of U.S. sanctions.

According to atimes.com; September 24, 2018: In September 2018, the law firm that conducted an investigation for Danske Bank estimated that the amount of suspicious transactions at the Estonian branch of the company was EUR 200,000,000,000. The money transited through the Estonian subsidiary of Danske Bank between 2007 and 2015.

According to rte.ie; September 21, 2018: As of September 2018, Danske Bank A/S is under investigation by Britain's National Crime Agency. The agency investigates the involvement of the United Kingdom concerning the connection of money laundering at Danske Bank.

According to the yle.fi; August 06, 2018: In the ongoing investigation of Danske Bank a new leak revealed that the sum subjected to money laundering is estimated to be around EUR 7,000,000,000. It is also reported that the money laundered through the Estonian branch of Danske Bank came from Russia, Moldova and Azerbaijan. Danske Bank has started a internal investigation; the results will be revealed in September, 2018.

According to the European Securities and Markets Authority; July 23, 2018: On July 23, 2018, Danske Bank A/S was fined EUR 495,000 by the European Securities and Markets Authority for negligently breaching the Credit Rating Agencies Regulation. Danske Bank A/S issued credit ratings between June, 2011 and August, 2016 without the authorization of the European Securities and Markets Authority. 

According to dr.dk, nyheder.tv2.dk and defensenews.com; July 03, 2018: In July, 2018, in the ongoing money laundering investigation of the Estonian branch of Danske Bank, a new leak revealed the amount of DKK 25,000,000,000 in addition to the previously discovered DKK 28,000,000,000, thus, creating a total amount of DKK 53,000,000. The new amount subjected to money laundering was revealed through 20 accounts which appear in bank statements received from 20 companies that had accounts in the Estonian branch, during different periods between 2007 and 2015. The suspicious amounts were channeled to Danske Bank Estonia from Moldova, Russia and Azerbaijan and into Europe. The Danish investigators are also examining the end-uses of the money laundered for the shipment of military materials through North Korea and Iran from December, 2009.

According to the United States -Colorado Public Employees' Retirement Association: June 16, 2023: On April 04, 2018, Danske Bank A/S was removed from the restricted (i.e. scrutinized) Israel companies list published by the Colorado Public Employees' Retirement Association. On September 22, 2017, Danske Bank A/S is placed on the restricted companies list published by the Colorado Public Employees' Retirement Association.

According to the United States-Illinois State Board of Investment; January 16, 2018: On June 30, 2017, Danske Bank is included in the prohibited list, deemed prohibited from investment for having ties with entities that boycott Israel. 

According to the United States-Illinois Investment Policy Board - Prohibited Investment List; Danske Bank is added to the Illinois Prohibited Investment List, deemed prohibited from investment.

According to danskebank.dk; December 21, 2017: On December 21, 2017, Danske Bank has agreed to pay the fine of DKK 12,500,000 for violating the anti-money laundering legislation. 

According to anklagemyndigheden.dk; December 21, 2017: On December 21, 2017, Danske Bank was fined DKK 12,500,000 for violating the Money Laundering Act by the State Prosecutor for Serious Economic and International Crime. The fine came as a result of a 2016 inspection conducted by the Financial Supervisory Authority of Denmark, which showed that Danske Bank has violated the Money Laundering Act. The bank failed to follow the rules in regard to supervising transactions to and from banks which provide services on Danske Bank's behalf.      

According to euobserver.com; October 13, 2017: The Tribunal de Grande Instance de Paris stated that EUR 15,000,000 of money from organized fraud and tax evasion in Russia were moved through Danske Bank Estonian Branch into France and other EU jurisdictions from 2008 to 2011 via multiple transactions in an organized manner.

According to news.err.ee; September 05, 2017: Between 2012 and 2014, Danske Bank permitted the Azerbaijani regime to send approximately USD 2,900,000,000 of bribe money through accounts in the bank’s Estonian branch to at least two European politicians, a journalist writing regime-friendly articles, companies selling luxury goods, and other influential individuals around the world, overriding money laundering regulations.

According to reuters.com; March 21, 2017: On March 20, 2017, Danske Bank A/S has agreed to cooperate in the investigation conducted by the authorities in Moldova and Latvia. Danske Bank is suspected of money laundering operations handled through their international branches. Between 2011 and 2014, over DKK 7,000,000,000 was transferred to accounts of Danske Bank A/S and another bank. Most of the transactions were made by Danske Bank's Estonian branch.

hit.profile_notes:
On July 25, 2018, the United States Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control imposed sanctions against Anni Beurklian. Anni Beurklian was a key component of a vast network procuring electronics on behalf of Syria’s Scientific Studies and Research Center (SSRC), the agency responsible for the development of Syria’s chemical weapons.

According to United States United States Attorney - District of Massachusetts; June 11, 2020: On June 11, 2020, filed a civil forfeiture action against Anni Beurklian and her husband Antoine Ajaka in connection with a scheme to smuggle goods out of the United States and to supply services to Syria. The United States also seized the U.S. website of the Syrian-based company Electronic Katranji Trading (“EKT”), ekt2.com, on probable cause that it was used to facilitate the illegal export of merchandise from the United States.The couple operated Top Tech US Inc. (“Top Tech”), a U.S. company, from the Waltham home. Beurklian, Ajaka and Top Tech were indicted in March 2018 on conspiracy to violate U.S. export laws and regulations, conspiracy to defraud the United States, smuggling U.S. goods out of the United States, illegally providing services to persons located in Syria, mail fraud, conspiracy to obstruct justice and obstruction of justice.

The civil forfeiture action and website seizure are pursuant to Title 19 of the United States Code, which provides that property used to facilitate the exporting or sending of merchandise from the United States contrary to law shall be seized and forfeited to the United States.

According to United States Department of State Directorate of Defense Trade Controls; November, 2019: On March 21, 2018 Anni Beurkl and her husband, Antoine Ajaka their company Top Tech US Inc, and a Syrian national Amir Katranji were indicted on conspiracy to violate U.S. export laws and regulations, conspiracy to defraud the United States, smuggling U.S. goods out of the United States, conspiracy to obstruct justice, and obstruction of justice. Beurklian, Ajaka, and Top Tech US Inc. also are charged with illegally providing services to persons located in Syria and mail fraud.

According to United States Attorney - District of Massachusetts; March 21, 2018: Anni Beurklian and her husband, Antoine Ajaka, their company Top Tech US Inc, and a Syrian national Amir Katranji were indicted on conspiracy to violate U.S. export laws and regulations, conspiracy to defraud the United States, smuggling U.S. goods out of the United States, conspiracy to obstruct justice, and obstruction of justice. Beurklian, Ajaka, and Top Tech US Inc. are also charged with illegally providing services to persons located in Syria and mail fraud. Beurklian and Ajaka previously fled the U.S. and have not returned. 

As alleged in the indictment, beginning no later than 2012 and continuing until Jan. 09, 2018, Beurklian and her husband operated an export business, Top Tech US Inc., out of their Waltham residence. The couple used their business to procure goods, including electronics, computer equipment, and electrical switches, from U.S. companies and export those goods out of the United States to customers in Lebanon and Syria. 

The indictment further alleges that in or about 2013, Ajaka and Beurklian began doing business with Katranji and supplying U.S. origin goods to EKT using Top Tech US. Ajaka and Beurklian knew that Katranji operated a business in Syria and that they were providing brokering services to Katranji and his Syrian company, EKT, by buying and shipping U.S. origin goods to EKT and its customers. EKT paid Ajaka and Beurklian more than USD 200,000 through Top Tech US bank accounts for their services. To conceal their illegal activity with EKT and evade the mandatory export filing requirement, Ajaka and Beurklian, with the knowledge and agreement of Katranji, falsified shipping paperwork and undervalued goods being shipped overseas directly to, or on behalf of, EKT.

He visited Balajiholydasindia.com and got the number of Jain who offered a package tour. The complainant then transferred INR 150,000 to Jain in instalments through different bank accounts. The accused then asked for the balance payment but the complainant said he will pay only after the flight ticket gets confirmed. The next day, Patel called up the complainant and said he is sending the flight ticket and demanded INR 100,000 towards the balance payment. The complainant transferred the money but he didn’t get the ticket. He then called up Jain but didn’t get any response. The complainant got suspicious and checked the invoice sent by the accused which turned out to be fake. The complainant said in his complaint that another citizen too was duped in a similar manner by the accused. He has lost INR 276,000.

hit.name: Michael David Taylor
hit.position_or_allegation: Fined USD 5,000 and suspended from association with any Financial Industry Regulatory Authority member in any capacity for three months for violating the Financial Industry Regulatory Authority rule - April 08, 2016.

details.enforcement: Debarred/Disciplined | US –Financial Industry Regulatory Authority | United States

hit.profile_notes: According to United States-Financial Industry Regulatory Authority; June 2016: On April 08, 2016, Michael David Taylor was assessed a deferred fine of USD 5,000 and suspended from association with any FINRA member in any capacity for three months. Without admitting or denying the findings, Taylor consented to the sanctions and to the entry of findings that he circumvented his member firm’s annuity replacement procedures by failing to identify and submit variable annuity purchases totaling approximately USD 700,000 as annuity replacements, even though each purchase was funded by the sale of another annuity. The findings stated that Taylor concealed the replacement transactions from the firm’s supervisory review by transferring the proceeds from the replaced annuity to a firm money market account in the customer’s name. After waiting approximately 30 to 60 days, Taylor then used the funds in the money market account to purchase the new variable annuity. Taylor further concealed that the annuity purchases were replacements by providing inaccurate information on the transaction documents he submitted to the firm and the annuity companies. Taylor earned approximately USD 18,000 in additional commissions by submitting the annuity purchases as new trades rather than as annuity replacements. Taylor subsequently repaid these commissions to the firm. The suspension is in effect from April 18, 2016 to July 17, 2016.

details.enforcement: Terrorism | PK-Federal Investigation Agency (FIA) - Govt. of Pakistan | Pakistan

hit.profile_notes:
According to the Federal Investigation Agency (FIA) - Govt. of Pakistan; June 2014: Anti Terrorism Act 1997 inspite of various shortcomings has provided effective mechanism to police stations to conduct surveillance of activists on Schedule-IV of the Act in order to curb and prevent acts of terrorism by members of proscribed organizations. Section-11EE prescribes restrictions on movements, residence & visits of these suspects. Section 11EE also states that suspects before leaving the area of residence have to seek prior permission of Officer In charge of Police Station. Their assets & sources of incomes will also be subject to investigation. ATA-1997 further provides that any person who violates any direction or order shall be punishable with an imprisonment of up to 3 years or fine or both. However, these provisions of ATA 1997 are not enforced effectively or uniformly. It is very rare to observe registration of cases against suspects u/s 11EE ATA 1997. CTW FIA has prepared the consolidated list of Activists on basis of data provided by CTD/CIDs and Home Departments.

Once all provinces have updated lists of Activists on Schedule-IV the Federal & Provincial Govts. may also consider some amendments in ATA in order to deny or restrict issuance of passports, arms licence, driving licence, credit card, internet usage etc to these suspects so that they cannot easily travel, associate, rent building, buy weapons/transport/ dual use chemicals, harbor terrorists, use internet etc, and conduct terrorist attacks freely.
